The core methodology begins with supervised Euclidean segmentation, which partitions an image into foreground and background based on color intensity thresholds. This step is foundational for detecting moving objects in a scene. Subsequently, shape descriptors derived from segmented regions are compared using a minimum distance classifier to assign object identities. The process relies on geometric properties such as boundary length and Freeman chain codes to encode object contours. These descriptors enable robust classification even under varying illumination. Finally, object trajectories are constructed by tracking centroids across frames, assuming consistent object identity and minimal occlusion. Each primitive operates within a layered architecture: segmentation provides input, classification assigns semantics, and trajectory generation offers spatiotemporal dynamics. Dualities emerge in how shape descriptors map to class labels and how centroid motion reflects physical movement. Failure modes include misclassification due to overlapping features, segmentation errors from lighting variation, and trajectory loss during occlusion or object disappearance.
